title: When benchmarking a reactive service against a blocking one, what mistakes make the comparison unfair? Explain coordinated omission, database saturation, connection pool sizing, and GC pressure from R2DBC tiny objects combined with an undersized young generation (`-Xmn`).
shortTitle: Reactive vs blocking benchmark mistakes — omission, DB saturation, pool sizing, GC pressure

s1_definition.profdef: Fair reactive-versus-blocking benchmarking requires eliminating four common distortions. Coordinated omission makes the closed-model generator hide tail latency equally but can flatter the reactive stack that queues internally. Database saturation means both stacks funnel into the same database, so you end up measuring the database, not the application model. Connection pool sizing must be matched and correct, because an undersized pool throttles the blocking stack while an oversized one saturates the database. And the reactive stack, especially with R2DBC, allocates many tiny short-lived objects per request, so an undersized young generation (`-Xmn`) causes frequent minor collections and GC pressure that unfairly penalises reactive.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine racing two delivery teams at National Bank of India — a blocking team and a reactive team — but the race is rigged in four sneaky ways. First, the stopwatch pauses whenever a team is stuck in traffic, so both look faster than they are (coordinated omission). Second, both teams must pass through the same narrow bank gate, so you are really timing the gate, not the teams (database saturation). Third, one team is given only two vans while the other has fifty, so of course one looks slow (connection pool sizing). Fourth, the reactive team's paperwork is thousands of tiny slips that fill the inbox instantly and force constant clean-ups, but only because the inbox was made too small (undersized young generation causing GC pressure). A fair race fixes all four before you believe any number.
s1_definition.oneliner: A fair reactive-versus-blocking benchmark must defeat coordinated omission, avoid measuring a saturated shared database, match and correctly size connection pools, and size the young generation so R2DBC's tiny-object allocation does not create unfair GC pressure.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Fair reactive-versus-blocking benchmarking requires eliminating four common distortions. Coordinated omission makes the closed-model generator hide tail latency equally but can flatter the reactive stack that queues internally. Database saturation means both stacks funnel into the same database, so you end up measuring the database, not the application model. Connection pool sizing must be matched and correct, because an undersized pool throttles the blocking stack while an oversized one saturates the database. And the reactive stack, especially with R2DBC, allocates many tiny short-lived objects per request, so an undersized young generation (`-Xmn`) causes frequent minor collections and GC pressure that unfairly penalises reactive.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine racing two delivery teams at National Bank of India — a blocking team and a reactive team — but the race is rigged in four sneaky ways. First, the stopwatch pauses whenever a team is stuck in traffic, so both look faster than they are (coordinated omission). Second, both teams must pass through the same narrow bank gate, so you are really timing the gate, not the teams (database saturation). Third, one team is given only two vans while the other has fifty, so of course one looks slow (connection pool sizing). Fourth, the reactive team's paperwork is thousands of tiny slips that fill the inbox instantly and force constant clean-ups, but only because the inbox was made too small (undersized young generation causing GC pressure). A fair race fixes all four before you believe any number.

**One line to remember:** A fair reactive-versus-blocking benchmark must defeat coordinated omission, avoid measuring a saturated shared database, match and correctly size connection pools, and size the young generation so R2DBC's tiny-object allocation does not create unfair GC pressure.

sections.s2_technical:
Coordinated omission bites both stacks but not equally. In a closed, wait-for-response load generator, each virtual user sends the next request only after the previous response returns, so a stall stops the generator and the tail is hidden. The reactive stack tends to queue work internally rather than block a thread, so under a closed model it can absorb bursts invisibly and report a flattering p99, while the blocking stack's thread exhaustion is more visible. The fix is an open, constant-arrival-rate generator like wrk2 or k6 that keeps sending on schedule, plus HdrHistogram's `recordValueWithExpectedInterval(value, expectedInterval)` so both stacks are measured against the same honest clock. If you compare a reactive p99 measured under coordinated omission against a blocking p99 measured honestly, you are comparing fiction to fact.

Database saturation is the most common way these benchmarks become meaningless. Both the blocking and reactive services ultimately send SQL to the same PostgreSQL, which has a finite number of CPU cores and a finite disk. If your load drives the database to one hundred percent CPU, then both stacks wait on the database and their latencies converge, so you are benchmarking PostgreSQL, not the application concurrency model. To compare the models fairly you must keep the database below saturation, or deliberately decide the experiment is about end-to-end throughput including the database and interpret the result accordingly. A clean way to isolate the application model is to stub the data access with a fixed-delay fake so both stacks hit an identical, unsaturated dependency, revealing how each handles concurrency rather than how PostgreSQL handles load.

Connection pool sizing must be matched and sane. The blocking stack uses a thread-per-request model with a JDBC pool such as HikariCP; a common formula is pool size near the number of cores times two plus the effective spindle count, and oversizing it does not help because the database cannot do more concurrent work than it has cores. The reactive stack uses R2DBC with its own connection pool, usually much smaller, because a handful of connections can multiplex many in-flight requests via non-blocking I/O. The mistake is giving the blocking stack a tiny pool so it queues, or giving either stack a pool so large it saturates the database. For a fair comparison you size each pool correctly for its model and verify that neither the pool nor the database is the artificial bottleneck, for example by confirming the database is not at one hundred percent and the pool is not fully exhausted during the run.

GC pressure is where reactive gets unfairly punished if you are careless. R2DBC and the reactive pipeline allocate a large number of tiny, short-lived objects per request — operator wrappers, subscriptions, signals, lambda captures and small buffers. These objects die young, which is normal and cheap if the young generation is large enough, because a minor collection reclaims them quickly. But if you run with an undersized young generation, for example a small `-Xmn`, the Eden space fills constantly, minor collections fire very frequently, and the per-request allocation churn turns into a storm of young collections that adds latency and burns CPU. This can make reactive look slower than blocking purely as a JVM-tuning artifact. The fix is to size the young generation generously so the high allocation rate of short-lived reactive objects is absorbed by infrequent, cheap minor collections, for example increasing `-Xmn` or letting an adaptive collector like G1 size the young generation, and to measure the allocation rate with `-Xlog:gc*` so you can see whether you are collector-bound rather than application-bound.

The senior-level nuance tying these together is that a benchmark comparing two architectures must hold everything else equal: same open-model generator, same unsaturated dependency, correctly sized pools for each model, and a JVM tuned so neither stack is starved of young-generation space. Only then does the number reflect the concurrency model rather than a misconfiguration. A further nuance is that reactive's advantage is specifically thread efficiency under high concurrency with blocking-style latency, so the benchmark should include enough concurrency to exercise that; at low concurrency blocking often wins on raw latency because it avoids the reactive overhead, and quoting a low-concurrency result as proof reactive is slower is just as misleading as the reverse.
sections.s3_banking:
National Bank of India is deciding whether to rewrite its account-lookup service from a blocking Spring MVC plus JDBC design to a reactive WebFlux plus R2DBC design. The first benchmark declared reactive twenty percent slower, and the team almost cancelled the rewrite. A review found all four classic mistakes.

Problem 1 — the benchmark used a closed JMeter run, so the reactive stack's internal queueing hid its true tail while the blocking stack's thread exhaustion was visible. This is coordinated omission, and the fix is an open constant-arrival-rate measurement with HdrHistogram expected-interval correction.

Problem 2 — both stacks hammered the same PostgreSQL to one hundred percent CPU, so both were really waiting on the database and the models were indistinguishable. This is database saturation, and to isolate the model we replace the real database with a fixed-delay fake repository that both stacks call identically.

Problem 3 — the blocking stack was given a two-connection pool while the reactive stack had a well-tuned one, so the blocking stack queued artificially. This is connection pool mis-sizing, and the fix is to size each pool correctly for its model and confirm neither is the bottleneck.

Problem 4 — the reactive run used a tiny young generation, so R2DBC's per-request tiny objects caused a storm of minor collections. This is GC pressure from undersized `-Xmn`, and the fix is to size the young generation for the reactive allocation rate and log GC to prove it.

The code will simulate the two stacks fairly: a `FixedDelayAccountRepository` that both stacks share so the dependency is identical and unsaturated, a `BlockingLookupService` using a sized thread pool, a `ReactiveLookupService` that allocates many tiny per-request objects like R2DBC would, and a `FairBenchmark` that drives both under an open-model schedule, records into HdrHistogram with expected-interval correction, and reports matched percentiles. A `FairBenchmarkDemo` main class runs both and prints the fair comparison.

sections.s4e_build:
```bash
# Build
mvn clean package

# FAIR run: ample young-gen so reactive tiny-object churn is cheap, GC logged
java -Xms4g -Xmx4g -Xmn2g \
     -Xlog:gc*:file=gc-fair.log:time,tags \
     -cp target/classes:$(cat cp.txt) com.bank.fair.FairBenchmarkDemo

# UNFAIR run (shows the trap): tiny young-gen punishes reactive with GC storms
java -Xms4g -Xmx4g -Xmn64m \
     -Xlog:gc*:file=gc-unfair.log:time,tags \
     -cp target/classes:$(cat cp.txt) com.bank.fair.FairBenchmarkDemo

# Compare minor-GC counts between gc-fair.log and gc-unfair.log
grep -c "Pause Young" gc-fair.log gc-unfair.log
```
sections.s5_journey:
The input is twenty thousand account-lookup requests for SAV2001 at a fixed schedule of one request every one hundred microseconds, run once through the blocking stack and once through the reactive stack, both against the same fixed-five-millisecond repository.

Step 1 — the benchmark computes a scheduled send time for each request from a fixed base, so request number i is scheduled at base plus i times one hundred microseconds. This is the open model: the schedule does not depend on when responses arrive.

Step 2 — for the blocking stack, each request is submitted to a correctly sized thread pool of cores-times-two threads. Each worker blocks five milliseconds in the shared repository and returns the balance. Because the pool is sized sanely and the repository is unsaturated, the stack processes the schedule without artificial queueing.

Step 3 — the benchmark measures latency from the scheduled send time, not from dispatch, and records it with `recordValueWithExpectedInterval` so any internal queueing during a slow moment is attributed honestly. The blocking histogram fills with values dominated by the five-millisecond dependency.

Step 4 — for the reactive stack, each request allocates thirty-two tiny Signal objects plus a couple of short-lived BigDecimal objects, mimicking R2DBC's per-request churn, then reads the same five-millisecond repository on a small event-loop pool. With an ample young generation these tiny objects die in a cheap minor collection, so GC barely registers.

Step 5 — the same open-model measurement records the reactive latencies. Because the dependency and the schedule are identical and the pools are each correctly sized, the reactive median sits close to the blocking median, around five milliseconds, with the tails reflecting each model's overhead rather than a rigged setup.

Step 6 — if you re-run the reactive stack with a tiny young generation, the thirty-two-objects-per-request churn fills Eden constantly, minor collections fire far more often, and the reactive p99 inflates — not because reactive is slower, but because the JVM was misconfigured. The gc logs make this visible, and the fair rules are logged as the conclusion.

```
Oct 20, 2026 11:58:14 PM com.bank.fair.FairBenchmarkDemo main
INFO: Blocking stack with CORRECTLY SIZED pool (cores*2)...
INFO: BLOCKING median=5.02ms p99=5.40ms p99.9=6.10ms
INFO: Reactive stack (few threads, many tiny objects per request)...
INFO: REACTIVE median=5.03ms p99=5.55ms p99.9=6.80ms
WARNING: Fair rules: open model, shared unsaturated repo, matched pools, ample young-gen (-Xmn) so R2DBC tiny objects don't skew GC.
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
When I benchmark a reactive stack against a blocking one, I treat the setup itself as the main risk, because four classic mistakes can make the result meaningless. The first is coordinated omission. A closed, wait-for-response generator stops sending during a stall, which hides the tail, and it hides it unevenly: the reactive stack queues work internally and looks flatteringly fast, while the blocking stack's thread exhaustion is more visible. So I always use an open, constant-arrival-rate generator like wrk2 or k6, and I record with HdrHistogram's expected-interval correction, so both stacks are measured against the same honest clock.

The second mistake is database saturation. Both stacks send SQL to the same database, and if I drive that database to a hundred percent CPU, both stacks simply wait on it and their latencies converge, so I am benchmarking PostgreSQL, not the concurrency model. To isolate the model I keep the database well below saturation, or I replace it with a fixed-delay fake that both stacks call identically, which reveals how each model handles concurrency rather than how the database handles load.

The third mistake is connection pool sizing. The blocking stack is thread-per-request with a JDBC pool, sized sensibly around cores times two, while the reactive stack uses a much smaller R2DBC pool because non-blocking I/O multiplexes many requests over few connections. If I give the blocking stack a tiny pool it queues artificially, and if I give either stack a huge pool it saturates the database. So I size each pool correctly for its model and confirm during the run that neither the pool nor the database is the artificial bottleneck.

The fourth mistake is the subtlest and it unfairly punishes reactive. R2DBC and the reactive pipeline allocate many tiny, short-lived objects per request — operator wrappers, subscriptions, signals, small buffers. That is cheap if the young generation is large, because a minor collection reclaims them instantly, but if I run with an undersized young generation, Eden fills constantly, minor collections fire in a storm, and the reactive p99 balloons purely as a JVM-tuning artifact. So I size the young generation generously for the reactive allocation rate and log GC to prove neither stack is collector-bound. At National Bank of India this review saved a project: our first benchmark called the reactive rewrite twenty percent slower, but it had a closed generator, a saturated database, a two-connection blocking pool, and a tiny young generation. Once I fixed all four, the two stacks were neck and neck at low concurrency and reactive pulled ahead under high concurrency, which is exactly the thread-efficiency advantage reactive is supposed to have. The principle I state in interviews is that an architecture benchmark is only trustworthy when everything except the architecture is held equal.
